Threat.value: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a childhood trauma of witnessing domestic violence, the trigger pattern is strongly male-linked ('being alone with men') but also includes 'being alone with women' without any corresponding formulation or symptom content explaining why both genders would be equivalently triggering. That broadens the trigger profile in a way that is hard to connect to the rest of the report, which is centered on interpersonal threat from others who might harm him rather than gender-nonspecific social presence.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Driving/being a passenger in a vehicle' is difficult to link to the reported trauma and the rest of the profile. No other trigger, threat, or memory item involves transport, accidents, escape, or vehicles, so this strategy appears to address a symptom domain not represented elsewhere in the five components.

vignette:
Tane is an 18-year-old American young man of Pacific Islander background who came to treatment after years of feeling as if danger could arrive without warning. He grew up in a home where, as a child, he repeatedly witnessed his mother being terrorized by a man who had been drinking. What stayed with him was not a single clean scene but flashes: the sour smell of alcohol filling a room, the sound of a door being shoved, the sight of an adult male body blocking the way out, and the feeling of being very small and unable to predict what would happen next. Even when he tries to describe it now, Tane says he can only get pieces. Large parts feel missing, and the parts he does recall come as disconnected fragments that do not fit into a full story. When those fragments surface, they do not feel distant; he is hit by the same terror he felt then.

Over time, certain moments in ordinary life began to carry the force of those childhood scenes. The smell of alcohol is especially potent, and being alone with men can make his body tense before he has had time to think. Even a bicycle can catch him off guard; seeing one or hearing it approach can pull up a jolt of fear tied to half-remembered childhood moments outside the house. These triggers do not just remind him in a mild way. They seem to pull memory toward him in fragments, and because the memory arrives in pieces, the trigger itself feels harder to make sense of and more dangerous the next time it appears.

He now works as a project manager, and the daily demands of coordinating people have become one of the places where his symptoms are most visible. If he has to meet a male vendor alone, or pass a coworker in the hall who smells faintly of alcohol from the night before, he becomes sharply alert. He watches men’s faces, posture, and movements for any sign that they might turn threatening. Ordinary office noises make him jump. Before settling at his desk or leaving a meeting room, he finds himself checking doors and locks repeatedly, as if failing to do so would leave him exposed. The bicycle rack outside the building has become another point of strain; even noticing the clustered bikes when he arrives can make him scan the area and feel as though something bad is about to happen.

Because these reactions feel so immediate, Tane has developed ways of getting through the day that bring short-term relief but narrow his life. After encounters that set him off, he smokes outside the office to calm down. He has also been drinking and using medication or drugs to blunt the aftereffects when the fear lingers into the evening. He avoids people more than he used to, especially situations where he might be alone with a man, and he has started structuring work so that conversations happen by message or with others present. His girlfriend has noticed that he withdraws after certain days and becomes difficult to reach.

The same pattern tightens once a memory has been stirred. When a smell or situation brings back one of those fragments, the terror returns so strongly that he reaches for whatever will shut it down fastest: a cigarette, alcohol, medication, distance from other people. Yet these efforts leave him more cut off and more vigilant. The more he avoids and numbs, the more uncertain the past feels, and the less complete his memory becomes, so that the next trigger lands as something sudden and unexplained. He has grown increasingly preoccupied with making sure doors and windows are locked, startling at ordinary sounds at home, and studying other people closely in public. That constant watchfulness means he notices every possible cue—men nearby, alcohol on someone’s breath, a bicycle passing—and each cue is given immediate importance.

In recent months this has begun to affect his work and relationship in ways he can no longer dismiss. He spends too much energy monitoring rooms instead of focusing on projects, and he sometimes rearranges meetings for reasons he cannot easily explain to colleagues. At home, he checks locks repeatedly before bed and remains keyed up if a sound catches him off guard. What finally brought him in was a recent day at work when the smell of alcohol on a client, the sight of a bicycle outside, and being briefly alone with another man in a conference room set off a rush of terror he could not contain. He left to smoke, later drank to settle himself, and was shaken by how quickly he had felt like a frightened child again. Tane is seeking help because he is afraid this fear is running his life, and because he wants, more than anything, to be able to remember what happened without feeling trapped inside it.
